en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Saṅghādisesa Offenses.
6. The Training Rule on Huts At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the monks of Āḷavī were having huts built by means of solicitation—huts that were ownerless, for their own private use, and of unlimited size.
They do not reach their goal.
They dwell full of begging and full of requests:
"Give us a man! Give us a male servant! Give us an ox! Give us a cart! Give us an axe! Give us a hatchet!"
“Give us an axe! Give us a spade! Give us a chisel! Give us creepers! Give us bamboo!
Give us *muñja* grass! Give us *pabbaja* grass! Give us grass! Give us clay!

People, distressed by this begging and distressed by these requests, became terrified and alarmed upon seeing the monks; they fled, went by other ways, turned their faces away, or even bolted the doors.
Seeing even a cow, they fled, thinking, "It is a monk.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having completed the rains retreat at Rājagaha, set out for Āḷavī.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at Āḷavī.
There, the Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Mahākassapa dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Āḷavī for alms.
When people saw the Venerable Mahākassapa, they were terrified, alarmed, and fled; some went by one way, others turned their faces another way, and some even bolted their doors.
Then, having walked for alms in Āḷavī and returned from his almsround after the meal, the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, formerly this Āḷavī was well-supplied with food, where alms were easy to obtain and it was easy to maintain oneself by gleaning and gathering;
but now this Āḷavī is short of food, where alms are difficult to obtain and it is not easy to maintain oneself by gleaning and gathering."
“Friends, what is the cause, what is the reason, why this Āḷavī is short of food, where alms are difficult to obtain, and it is not easy to subsist by gathering gleanings?
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Venerable Mahākassapa.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, having stayed at Rājagaha for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Āḷavī.
Wandering by stages on his journey, he arrived at Āḷavī.
There, the Blessed One stayed at the Aggāḷava Shrine in Āḷavī.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Mahākassapa reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks of Āḷavī:
"Is it true, monks, that you are having kutis built by means of solicitation, for which no owner exists, dedicated to yourselves, and of unlimited size?"
They do not reach their goal. You dwell full of begging and full of requests:
“Give us a man! Give us a man’s helper! … [and so on] … give us grass! Give us clay!”
“Are people not distressed by begging, distressed by requests, and alarmed, terrified, and fleeing upon seeing monks;
do they not go by another way, turn their faces away, or even bolt the door,
and flee even at the sight of a cow, thinking it is a monk?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, have huts built by means of requests, for which there is no owner, intended for yourselves, and of unlimited size? This is not fitting, foolish men…” [and so on].
Those [desires] do not lead to the ultimate goal.
You will dwell full of begging and full of requests:
"Give us a man! Give us a man-servant! ... give us grass! give us clay!"
“Foolish men, this will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
‘In the past, bhikkhus, two brothers who were seers lived depending upon the river Gaṅgā.’”
Then, monks, the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha, having crossed the river Gaṅgā, approached the junior seer;
having approached him, he encircled the junior seer seven times with his coils and stood there,
spreading a great hood over his head.
Then, monks, because of that fear of the nāga, the junior seer became thin, haggard, discolored, sallow, and his veins stood out upon his body.
The senior seer saw the junior seer— thin, haggard, discolored, sallow, and with his veins standing out upon his body—
and having seen him, he said this to the junior seer:
“Sir, why are you so thin, haggard, discolored, and pale, with your veins showing all over your body?

“Sir, here the Naga king named Maṇikaṇṭha, having crossed the river Gaṅgā, approached me. Having approached, he encircled me seven times with his coils and stood there raising a great hood over my head.
It is from fear of that Naga, sir, that I am so thin, haggard, discolored, and pale, with my veins showing all over my body.”
“But do you wish, sir, that the nāga should not come?
“Yes, sir, I wish that the nāga should not come.
“But do you see anything, sir, belonging to that nāga?”
‘“Sir, I see a jewel fastened around his neck.
“In that case, sir, ask that nāga for the jewel, saying:
‘Sir, give me the jewel.’”’
“I have need of a jewel.
Then, monks, the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha, having crossed the river Gaṅgā, approached the younger seer; having approached, he stood to one side.
As he was standing to one side, monks, the younger seer said this to the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha:
“Sir, give me the jewel;
I have need of the jewel.
Then, monks, the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha—
“A monk is asking for a jewel; the monk has need of a jewel,” he thought, and he went there immediately.
A second time, monks, the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha crossed the river Gaṅgā and approached the younger seer.
The younger seer saw the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the royal nāga Maṇikaṇṭha:
“Sir, give me the jewel;
I have need of the jewel.”
Then, monks, the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha, thinking, “The monk asks for the jewel;
the monk has need of the jewel,” turned back right there.
For a third time, monks, the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha crossed the river Gaṅgā.
Then, monks, the younger seer saw the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha crossing the river Gaṅgā.
Having seen him, he said this to the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha:
“Sir, give me the jewel.”
“I have need of the jewel.
Then, monks, the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha addressed the younger seer in verses:
“I have abundant and excellent food and drink;”
The cause for the arising of this jewel is this:
I will not give it to you, for you are an excessive beggar,
nor will I come to your hermitage.
Like a dog with hands washed clean of gravel,
you frighten me while begging for a stone;
I will not give that to you, for you beg too much.
"Nor will you come to my hermitage.
Then, monks, the Naga king Maṇikaṇṭha, thinking, "The monk asks for the jewel;
the monk has need of the jewel," departed.
Thus he departed and did not return again.

Then, monks, because of no longer seeing that beautiful nāga, the younger seer became even more emaciated, haggard, and discolored; he grew pale and yellowish, and his veins stood out all over his body.
The elder seer, monks, saw the younger seer becoming even more emaciated, haggard, and discolored, pale and yellowish, with his veins standing out all over his body.
Having seen him, he said this to the junior seer:
“Sir, why are you even more emaciated, haggard, discolored, and pale, with veins showing all over your body?
“Sir, it is because I have not seen that beautiful elephant that I am even more emaciated, haggard, discolored, and pale, with veins showing all over my body.”
Then, monks, the elder seer addressed the younger seer with a verse:
“One should not beg from one whom one wishes to love;
by excessive begging, one becomes a stranger.”
“The Nāga was asked for his jewel by the brahmin,
and he simply vanished from sight.
For even among those beings who are animals, monks, a request is unpleasant and a solicitation is unpleasant.
How much more so, then, for those who have become human?
Once upon a time, monks, a certain monk was dwelling on the slopes of the Himalayas in a certain forest thicket.
Not far from that forest thicket, monks, there was a large, low-lying marsh.
Then, monks, that great flock of birds, having foraged for food in that pond during the day, would return in the evening to that forest thicket to roost.
Then, monks, that monk, distressed by the noise of that flock of birds, approached me; having approached and paid homage to me, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, monks, I said this to that monk:
“Is it bearable, monk? Is it sustainable?
Have you come along this road without excessive fatigue?
And from where, monk, have you come?”
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is sustainable, Blessed One.
And I have come along this road, Bhante, without fatigue.
There, Bhante, on the slope of the Himalayas, is a great forest grove.”
"Moreover, venerable sir, not far from that grove there was a large, low-lying marsh.
Then, venerable sir, a great flock of birds, having foraged during the day at that marsh, would come to that grove in the evening to roost.
It was from there, Blessed One, that I came."
“‘I am distressed by the sound of that flock of birds.
‘But do you wish, monk, for the non-arrival of that flock of birds?
‘I do wish, Blessed One, for the non-arrival of that flock of birds.’”
“In that case, bhikkhu, go there, enter that forest grove, and during the first watch of the night, call out three times with a cry:
‘Listen, worthy birds, as many as have taken up residence in this forest grove; I have need of a wing.’”
‘Sirs, please give me each one alms-bowl.
During the middle watch of the night… and during the last watch of the night, you should announce this three times.”
“Listen to me, worthy birds, as many as have taken up residence in this forest grove: I have need of a leaf.
Let each of you, worthy sirs, give me a leaf.”
Then, monks, that monk went there, entered deep into that grove, and during the first watch of the night, three times he called out with a voice:
“Listen to me, sirs, you birds who have taken up residence in this grove; I have need of a wing.”
"May each of you, sirs, give me one alms-bowl.
During the middle watch of the night...
and during the last watch of the night, he made this proclamation three times:
"Listen to me, worthy birds, as many as have taken up residence in this forest grove: I have need of a leaf.
May each of you, worthy ones, give me a leaf."
Then, monks, that flock of birds, thinking,
“The monk is asking for an almsbowl; the monk has need of an almsbowl,” departed from that forest thicket.
Thus he departed and did not return again.
For even those animals, monks, found such begging and such entreaty unpleasant;
how much more so, then, for those who have become human?
“Bhikkhus, once in the past, the father of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla addressed the clansman Raṭṭhapāla with this verse:
‘I do not know you,
Raṭṭhapāla, nor do many people.’”
“They come together and entreat me;
why do you not entreat me?
“A beggar is disliked.”
"One who does not grant what is requested becomes unloved; therefore, I do not ask you for it,
lest I incur your displeasure."
For indeed, monks, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla would speak thus even to his own father;
how much more so, then, would one person speak to another?
Monks, the wealth accumulated by householders is difficult to amass and difficult to guard, even when it has been gathered.
In this matter, you foolish men, even though you have accumulated wealth that is so difficult to carry off and so hard to guard, you will dwell full of begging and full of requests:
"Give us a man! Give us a servant! Give us an ox! Give us a cart! Give us an axe! Give us a hatchet!
Give us an adze! Give us a spade! Give us a chisel! Give us a creeper! Give us a bamboo!"
“Give me muñja grass! Give me pabbaja grass! Give me grass! Give me clay!
“This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:”

“Now, when a monk is having a hut built by means of a formal request, it should be built for himself without an owner and within the proper measurements. Herein, these are the measurements: twelve spans long according to the span of the Sugata, and seven spans across.
Monks must be brought along for the inspection of the site. Those monks must designate the site as one that is free from harm and has space on all sides.”

“If a monk, in a site that is contested and not cleared of obstacles, should have a hut built by means of begging for materials, or fail to have monks brought along for the designation of the site, or should exceed the prescribed measurement, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
“By means of begging for materials” means:
having begged for himself, [he obtains] a man, a male servant, a bull, a cart, an axe, a hatchet, an adze, a spade, a chisel, a creeper, bamboo, *muñja* grass, *pabbaja* grass, grass, or clay.
"A hut" means it is either plastered on the inside, or plastered on the outside, or plastered on both the inside and the outside.
"By one who has it built" means:
Either doing it oneself or causing it to be done.
"Ownerless" means that there is no other owner whatsoever— neither a woman nor a man, neither a householder nor one gone forth.
"Attuddesa" means for one's own benefit.
It should be made according to the proper measure.
In this regard, the measurement is as follows: twelve spans long according to the Sugata-span;
and seven spans across, according to the outer measurement.
"By internal measurement.
"The monks should be brought for the designation of the site" means that the monk who is building the hut,
having cleared the site for the hut, should approach the Saṅgha with his upper robe arranged over one shoulder.
Having paid homage at the feet of the elder bhikkhus, sitting on his heels with his hands joined in reverential salutation, he should speak to them thus:
"Venerable sirs, I wish to have a hut built by means of solicitation, for my own use and without an owner.
Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha to inspect the site for the hut."
It should be requested a second time;
it should be requested a third time.
If the entire Saṅgha is able to inspect the site for the hut, the entire Saṅgha should inspect it.

If the entire Saṅgha is not able to inspect the site for the hut, those monks who are experienced and competent to determine whether there is harm or no harm, and whether it has an open space around it or not, should be requested and appointed.
"And thus, monks, they should be appointed.
An experienced and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha: [The formal motion follows]"
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk, named so-and-so, desiring to have a hut built by means of solicitation for himself, without an owner and for his own use,
requests the Saṅgha for the inspection of the site for the hut.’
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the bhikkhus named so-and-so and so-and-so to inspect the site for a hut for the bhikkhu named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me.
This monk, named so-and-so, desiring to have a hut built by means of a formal request, for himself and without an owner,
requests the Saṅgha to inspect the site for the hut.
The Saṅgha appoints the monks named so-and-so and so-and-so to inspect the site for the hut for this monk, named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable ones approve of the appointment of the monks [named] So-and-so and So-and-so to inspect the site for the hut of the monk [named] So-and-so, let them remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The monks [named] So-and-so and So-and-so have been appointed by the Saṅgha to inspect the site for the hut of the monk [named] So-and-so.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent;
thus do I hold it.

Those monks who have been appointed should go there and inspect the site for the hut, determining whether it involves harm to living beings or not, and whether it has sufficient space around it or not.
If it is a site with living beings and lacks space on all sides, one should say, "Do not build here.
If it is a site free from living beings and has space on all sides, one should inform the Saṅgha:
"It is free from living beings and has space on all sides."

That monk who intends to build a hut should approach the Saṅgha, adjust his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the senior monks, squat on his heels, raise his joined palms, and speak thus:
“Venerable sirs, I desire to build a hut by means of solicitation for myself, without an owner.
Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha to designate a site for the hut.”
A second time she should be asked;
a third time she should be asked.
An experienced and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
This monk named so-and-so wishes to have a hut built by means of solicitation for himself, as an ownerless structure intended for his own use.
He requests the Saṅgha for the designation of a site for the hut.”
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha assign a site for a hut to the monk named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
This monk named so-and-so, desiring to have a hut built by means of a formal request, intends to build one that is ownerless and for his own use.
He requests the Saṅgha to designate a site for the hut.
The Saṅgha designates a site for the hut for the monk named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable one approves of the assignment of a site for a hut to the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has assigned a site for a hut to the monk named so-and-so.
“The Saṅgha consents, therefore it is silent;
thus do I understand this.
This is called *sārambha*.
Or it may be the dwelling place of ants, or the dwelling place of termites, or the dwelling place of rats, or the dwelling place of snakes,
or the dwelling place of scorpions, or the dwelling place of centipedes, or the dwelling place of elephants,
or the dwelling place of horses, or the dwelling place of lions, or the dwelling place of tigers.
It is either the lair of leopards, or the lair of bears, or the lair of hyenas,
or the lair of whatever other animals belonging to the animal realm;
or it is dependent on stored grain, or dependent on fresh grain, or dependent on a slaughterhouse, or dependent on a place of execution.
It is either dependent on a charnel ground, or dependent on a park, or dependent on a royal compound,
or dependent on an elephant stable, or dependent on a horse stable, or dependent on a prison, or dependent on a tavern,
or dependent on a slaughterhouse, or dependent on a street, or dependent on a crossroads.
It is either dependent on a dwelling, dependent on an assembly hall, or dependent on a place of recreation.
This is called "with encroachment.
This is called "without space."
It is not possible to go around it with a cart as it is yoked, nor to go around it on all sides by means of a ladder.
This is called "without a walkway.
"Without injury" means that it is not the dwelling place of ants, nor the dwelling place of termites, nor the dwelling place of mice.
It is not the abode of snakes, nor the abode of scorpions, nor the abode of centipedes … [and so on] … nor does it depend upon a thoroughfare.
This is called "uninhabited. It is called "with a surrounding space."
It is possible to go around it with a yoked cart, or to go all around it by means of a ladder. This is called "with space on all sides.
"By one's own request" means having requested for oneself a man, a male servant, and so forth, or even clay.
A "hut" (kuṭi) means it is either plastered inside, or plastered outside, or plastered both inside and outside. "Should cause to be made" means:
He either builds it himself or has it built. Or,
without having the monks approve the site for the dwelling, he either builds it or has it built, exceeding the measurement for the site,

even by as much as the tip of a hair, either in length or in width— having failed to have the site for the hut approved by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma)— in the act of doing so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When one morsel has not yet arrived, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
When that morsel has arrived, there is an offense of saṅghādisesa.
"Saṅghādisesa" means:
... [as before] ... for that reason also it is called a *saṅghādisesa*.
If a monk builds a hut on an unassigned site, involving destruction of vegetation, and lacking a space around it, he commits one offense of *saṅghādisesa* and two offenses of *dukkaṭa*.
If a monk builds a hut on an unassigned site, involving destruction of vegetation, but with a space around it, he commits one offense of *saṅghādisesa* and one offense of *dukkaṭa*.

If a bhikkhu builds a hut on an unassigned site, where no harm will be done, and which lacks space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) and one offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If a bhikkhu builds a hut on an unassigned site, where no harm will be done, and which has space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension.
If a bhikkhu builds a hut on an assigned site, where harm will be done, and which lacks space on all sides, he commits two offenses of wrong-doing.
If a bhikkhu builds a hut on a site that has been designated, where harm will be caused, and which lacks a space for walking around, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If a bhikkhu builds a hut on a site that has been designated, where no harm will be caused, but which lacks a space for walking around, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If a bhikkhu builds a hut on a site that has been designated, where no harm will be caused, and which has a space for walking around, there is no offense.

If a bhikkhu builds a hut that exceeds the proper measure, involves destruction of living beings, and lacks space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) and two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If a bhikkhu builds a hut that exceeds the proper measure, involves destruction of living beings, but has space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing.

If a bhikkhu builds a hut that exceeds the proper measure, does not involve destruction of living beings, but lacks space on all sides, he commits one offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing.
If a bhikkhu builds a hut that exceeds the proper measure, where no harm is caused and there is sufficient space around it, he commits an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
If a bhikkhu builds a hut of the proper measure, where harm is caused and there is no space around it, he commits two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If a bhikkhu builds a hut of the proper measure, where harm is caused but there is sufficient space around it, he commits an offense of wrong-doing.
If a bhikkhu builds a hut that is within the prescribed measure, involves no harm to living beings, and lacks a space for walking around, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If a bhikkhu builds a hut that is within the prescribed measure, involves no harm to living beings, and includes a space for walking around, there is no offense.

If a bhikkhu builds a hut on a site not formally authorized, which exceeds the prescribed measure, involves harm to living beings, and lacks a space for walking around, he commits two offenses of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa) and two offenses of wrong-doing.
If a bhikkhu builds a hut on an unannounced site, exceeding the proper measure, involving destruction, and with space for a walk-around, he incurs two offenses: one *saṅghādisesa* and one *dukkaṭa*.

If a bhikkhu builds a hut on an unannounced site, exceeding the proper measure, not involving destruction, and without space for a walk-around, he incurs two offenses: one *saṅghādisesa* and one *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikkhu builds a hut on an unannounced site, exceeding the proper measure, not involving destruction, and with space for a walk-around, he incurs two *saṅghādisesa* offenses.

If a bhikkhu builds a hut on a site that has been designated, of the proper measure, involving destruction of living beings, and lacking a space for walking around, he commits two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If a bhikkhu builds a hut on a site that has been designated, of the proper measure, involving destruction of living beings, but with a space for walking around, he commits one offense of wrong-doing.

If a bhikkhu builds a hut on a site that has been designated, of the proper measure, not involving destruction of living beings, but lacking a space for walking around, he commits one offense of wrong-doing.
If a bhikkhu builds a hut on a site that has been authorized, to the proper measure, where no harm will be done, and which has space on all sides, there is no offense.
A bhikkhu gives an instruction:
"Build a hut for me."

If they build a hut for him on a site that has not been formally designated, where harm will be caused, and which lacks space on all sides, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) and two offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
… [omission] … where harm will be caused, but which has space on all sides, there is an offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing.
… [omission] … where no harm will be caused, but which lacks space on all sides, there is an offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing. … [omission] …
If it is without a foundation and lacks space on all sides, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A bhikkhu gives an instruction:
"Build a hut for me."

If they build a hut for him on a site that has been designated, where harm will be caused, and which lacks space on all sides, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for two [persons] …pe… where harm will be caused,
but which has space on all sides, there is an offense of wrong-doing …pe… where no harm will be caused,
but which lacks space on all sides, there is an offense of wrong-doing …pe…
If it is on ground that has not been cleared and is surrounded by space, there is no offense.
A bhikkhu gives instruction:
"Build a hut for me."

If they build a hut for him that exceeds the proper measure, involves destruction of living beings, and lacks space on all sides, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*) and two offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
… [omission] … If it involves destruction of living beings but has space on all sides, there is an offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing.
… [omission] … If it does not involve destruction of living beings but lacks space on all sides, there is an offense entailing suspension and one offense of wrong-doing. … [omission] …
If it is without a foundation and lacks a space for walking around, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A bhikkhu gives an instruction:
"Build a hut for me."

If they build him a hut that is within the proper measure, involves destruction of living beings, and lacks space on all sides, there is an offense of wrong-doing for two [persons] …pe… if it involves destruction of living beings but has space on all sides,
there is an offense of wrong-doing …pe… if it does not involve destruction of living beings but lacks space on all sides, there is an offense of wrong-doing …pe…
If it is on ground that is not cleared and has space around it, there is no offense.
A bhikkhu gives an instruction:
"Build a hut for me."

If they build a hut for him on a site not formally authorized, exceeding the proper dimensions, involving destruction, and lacking space on all sides, there is an offense of two *saṅghādisesas* and two *dukkaṭas*.
… [and so on] … if it involves destruction but has space on all sides, there is an offense of two *saṅghādisesas* and one *dukkaṭa*.
… [and so on] … if it does not involve destruction but lacks space on all sides, there is an offense of two *saṅghādisesas* and one *dukkaṭa*. … [and so on] …
If it is without a foundation and lacks space on all sides, there is an offense of two *saṅghādisesas*.
A monk gives an instruction:
"Build a hut for me."
